Field notes · Kestrel Bay

The board on the wall

For forty years the ferry terminal ran its day on a painted board and a handful of magnets. When the system replaced it, everyone kept walking to that wall.

Mira Calder · ~1,500 words · demo piece, fictional subject

At ten to six in the summer the magnets are warm. The board sits on the back wall of Terminal 4 beside the window, and the sun gets to it first, so if you come in early and put your hand flat on it to steady yourself on the way past, the little discs have held the heat from the glass. Nobody ever said to touch the board. People did.

It was painted steel with a brass rail along the bottom, and it had been there longer than anyone working there. Two boats, three crews, one that's always in the yard. That was the whole problem the board solved, and the scheduler on the 06:40 said it that way to anyone new who asked how a ferry terminal works.

A schedule is not a list of sailings. It is an argument about who is where, and the board was the form that argument took. Everybody in the building could read the state of it without asking anybody for anything.

The colors

Blue meant a vessel on its normal rotation. Red meant a vessel that could not sail — in the yard, or waiting on a survey, or under an inspection nobody had finished arguing about. White meant a crew change that had not settled yet, so the magnet might move before the morning was out. The columns were days. A red magnet in Tuesday's column was a boat out of the water on Tuesday, and you could see from the doorway where the gap was and who would have to cover it.

The red one had a chip in it, a piece gone from the lower corner since about 1998, and that chip was information too. It told you which red magnet was the long-standing yard vessel rather than whatever had broken this week.

There were rules about who could move them. Any scheduler could move a blue or a white. Only the duty superintendent could move a red, and if you moved a red you said so out loud, because moving a red magnet meant telling somebody a boat was not coming.

"That was the whole permission system. It was a rule about speech, not about access. If the wrong person moved a red, somebody would say who moved the Cormorant? and you'd find out in about ninety seconds."

The meeting

The replacement had been coming for years. Grant money, an audit recommendation, the usual weather. What made it happen when it did was a retirement: the man who kept the board was leaving, and the authority decided the knowledge should not leave with him. Get it out of his head and into a database. That was the sentence in the paper.

The meeting had five people in it. The superintendent, the operations manager, two schedulers, and a clerk taking notes. The superintendent did not argue against the system. He asked one question, and nobody answered it.

"Fine. But tell me who's allowed to move the red ones."

The manager said something about permissions and roles. The superintendent said, right, and then said, so tell me what the system calls a yard day. There was a pause in the room of the kind that gets written into the minutes as discussion. The clerk wrote the question in the open-items column, where it stayed.

The system was correct. This matters, and it is easy to lose when you are telling a story about something being taken down. It held the rotations, the crew assignments, the yard schedule, the survey dates, and the reasons. It kept a record of who changed what, which the board had never done except in the form of somebody shouting across an office. It printed a daily sheet, and it could tell you in March what had sailed in November.

What it could not do was sit on a wall.

05:40

The third morning after the cutover, a relief vessel came in early and the deckhand on duty needed to know whether he was going out on the second sailing. Deck crew never had logins. There had been no reason for them to have logins; the board was on the wall and the wall was in the room they were already standing in.

So he walked to the wall. There was a screen there now, turned off, and the office was empty at twenty to six. He went and found the clerk.

That was not a system failure. Nothing was down. Nothing was wrong in the database, and if you had asked the vendor they would have shown you the sailing list, correct, on a screen, behind a login, in an office, at an hour when the person who needed it was on a dock in the dark. It was a room failure.

"Everybody who needed the board could read it from the doorway. Only some of them could log in."

Eleven days, and a printout

The yard foreman asked whether the daily sheet could be printed and stuck on the wall. It could, and it was, and that continued for a month. Everybody called it a temporary measure, including the people who knew it was not.

In the yard the loss was specific. A yard day on the board had been the red magnet with the chip in it, hanging in a column where you could see it from the door. In the system it was a status code behind a login the yard never had a reason to hold. The foreman's printout was not nostalgia. It was the only way his crew could see the week without asking an office for it.

And for the first two weeks, people kept walking to that wall. Even the ones who had asked for the system. They would cross the room, stop, stand in front of a screen that was turned off, and then laugh at themselves and go back to a terminal. Nobody mentioned it in the meeting. It happened every morning.

The eleven days are not really the story. The system was new, the terminal was learning it, and things were slower the way anything is slower when the people doing it are reading instead of remembering. What the eleven days showed was where the knowledge had actually been living. It had not been living in the superintendent's head, which was the assumption in the paper. It had been living on a wall, in a form anyone in the building could read without being anyone in particular.

The rail

They took the board down in pieces. The superintendent kept the brass rail off the bottom of it, the one the magnets parked on overnight, and it is on a shelf in his office now, with nothing on it and nothing near it.

He was asked about it once, in the way people ask about objects in offices. He said, I could read it from the door, and then he went on to something else.

It did not sound like sentiment at the time and it does not read like it now. He was explaining what the rail was for. From the door, before the lights were on, before anybody had said good morning: how many magnets were not in a column. That was the number the rail held, and it was the first number of the day, and for forty years it was available to everyone who walked in, whether or not they had been given a password.

The system has that number too. It is on a dashboard, and it is accurate, and it is a great deal better than a board at everything a board was never going to be good at. To see it you go to a screen, and you are known to it, and if you are a deckhand at twenty to six on a dock with the water going out, you are neither.

Some things in a workplace are not storage. They are the part of the work that lets a person who is not in the meeting know what is happening in it. That is what was on the wall, and it is what the open-items column in the clerk's notes was never going to hold.
